dedupe_keys.name: england summer 2019 effects of hot weather on hospitals from frontline staff interviews

description: This case study examines how very hot weather in summer 2019 affected hospitals in England, their staff and the safety of care. The authors, researchers at the UK Health Security Agency and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine, interviewed 14 National Health Service professionals, including clinicians, facilities managers and emergency preparedness, resilience and response staff, after a pre-interview survey, and analysed the answers thematically; the work is published as an open-access journal article. Coverage is hospitals in England during the 2019 hot spells. The article is free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution licence; the interview data are not published. Caveats: the sample is small and qualitative, and costs of the impacts were not measured. The study found that hot weather caused significant disruption to services, facilities and equipment, discomfort for staff and patients and an acute rise in admissions; awareness of the Heatwave Plan for England and heat-health alerts varied between clinical and non-clinical staff; and responses were complicated by competing priorities such as infection control, the use of electric fans and patient safety. Simulation uses: qualitative evidence on failure modes of hospital buildings and operations under heat, for framing hospital resilience and adaptation models. Related records: the British Columbia heatwave simulation (case_study-british-columbia-2021-heatwave-acute-care-des) quantifies a heat surge in acute care.
